meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle. It paraphrases George Bernard Shaw's 1903 maxim “He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches” in Man and Superman.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — actually George Bernard Shaw
answer.sourceLine: Aristotle never wrote this. The line is a light modern paraphrase of Shaw’s aphorism “He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches,” printed under “Education” in the Maxims for Revolutionists ↗ appended to Man and Superman (1903). It is a deliberately provocative jab, not a considered verdict on teaching.

source.excerpt: He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches.
trail: The primary text: Shaw’s Maxims for Revolutionists ↗ prints the line verbatim under the heading “Education.”
Phrases.org.uk ↗ traces the saying to Shaw’s Man and Superman (1903) and gives the original wording.
The History Room ↗ notes the “Aristotle” version does not appear in his surviving texts and reads as a back-formation from Shaw.
source.excerptNote: Shaw’s original wording. The familiar form — “Those who can, do; those who cannot, teach” — is a later paraphrase that swaps his singular “he who” for a plural “those who.”
source.rightsNote: Shaw’s Man and Superman, containing the original maxim, was first published in 1903 — long before the 1931 US copyright cutoff — so the source text is in the public domain. The popular “Those who can, do” form is an anonymous later paraphrase of that public-domain line.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish dramatist and critic whose plays — Man and Superman, Pygmalion, Major Barbara — married sharp wit to social argument. He appended satirical aphorisms, the “Maxims for Revolutionists,” to Man and Superman in 1903; the teaching jab is one of them. Shaw won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.

copyAttribution: Original wording: "He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches." —George Bernard Shaw, Man and Superman (1903). Not Aristotle.

misattribution.heading: How Aristotle got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is routinely pinned on Aristotle in memes and quote sites, but it is neither his wording nor his idea — it is Shaw’s, paraphrased.

items.why: No such line exists in Aristotle’s surviving works; commentators note ↗ the “Aristotle” version is phrased to echo Shaw and appears nowhere in his texts. Aristotle’s Metaphysics in fact argues the near-opposite — that being able to teach is a mark of true knowledge.
Shaw printed “He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches” under “Education” in the Maxims for Revolutionists ↗ (1903).

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is Shaw’s 1903 maxim — “He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches” ↗ — lightly reworded; Aristotle has nothing to do with it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Shaw meant the line as provocation, not sociology. It sits among the “Maxims for Revolutionists,” a string of deliberately barbed aphorisms he attached to Man and Superman — the voice is that of the play’s firebrand John Tanner, a talker more than a doer.
Stripped of that satirical frame and re-pointed at schoolteachers, the maxim became a standalone insult, then drifted onto Aristotle as feel-good misattribution took hold online.
